newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-Lower kiwi dlr no panacea for NZ wool sector.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lower kiwi dlr no panacea for NZ wool sector.

text.p: A big "kiwi" dollar dive traditionally has New Zealand farmers rushing to buy new cars but experts doubt it will translate into significantly higher wool prices at the season's first sales on Thursday.

Kai Tovgaard, vice president of the Wool Exporters Council, has called the kiwi's fall a "dream come true" but others are sceptical, saying the nightmare of a never ending slide in real prices is unlikely to be significantly reversed.
"No one is rushing in and paying a lot more for wool," said President of the Wool Exporters Council, Don Quested.
"There hasn't been a dramatic influx of new business since the dollar has come down. Our clients overseas have been telling us for some time that our wool is too dear," he told Reuters.

"Our growers in New Zealand don't recognise that. It's partly to do with the big lift in our currency in the last couple of years. But our clients are still saying our wool should be cheaper in their currencies."
The kiwi dollar has fallen over 10 percent from its peak of 71.5 U.S. cents seen in November and even more against sterling. Its Trade-Weighted Index has dropped 7.0 percent since March.
The wool market indicator ended the 1996/97 season at NZ$4.63, one cent below the previous season's close.
But the average price was down 10 percent for the year.
Prices for wool types diverged sharply last year as China appeared to switch preference for the mainly Australian-produced finer wools away from New Zealand's coarse varieties.
The New Zealand market was heavily influence by the slowdown in Chinese buying, by far its largest customer. Sales to China fell to 50,140 tonnes from 67,300 tonnes the previous season.

Nick Nicholson, executive manager of the Wool Exporters Council said the first wool sales in Christchurch and Napier would be "a real acid test for the market" because of the large amount of wool on offer during what is normally a quiet time.
"Exporters would view any price direction with great caution despite the recent drop in the value of the New Zealand dollar.
"There's no doubt the current devaluation (depreciation) of our dollar is good news for the wool industry," he said.
But he said buyers may be reluctant to commit themselves in the hope of further gains from currency movements while sellers could hold back in hope of the dollar trending still lower.
"If structural change is occuring there, then it really is to the detriment of New Zealand's market there and to the advantage of Australia."
Quested said hopes were being pinned on the the European market lifting from its doldrums, for which there is no evidence, and the lifting of currency restrictions in Iran.
"If they were to come back into the market to their normal (level), that could make a significant influence," Quested said.
"What we really need is increased demand and we will get the benefits of the lower currency," he said.
Lincoln University wool science lecturer Hedley Sanderson expects exporters who have sold forward to make windfall gains and those gains would eventually be reflected in auction prices.
However, he said the problems for course wool producers may be long-term and demand might continue to be weak.
Much would depend on China where problems over the domestic economy, overproduction, and currency limits were improving.

"The thing that concerns me is the whispers I've heard about possible structural changes in the types of wool that China is purchasing, particularly for our huge hand knitting yarn market there -- that they may be moving finer."
Sanderson said farm returns for coarse wool had been trending down for 10 years and he expects finer wools to maintain their margin.
New Zealand farmers would continue to produce coarse wools because of good returns from the meat from crossbred sheep and the long time it took to change out of the market.
"The mood is resigned to prices in the foreseeable future to being not much higher than they are now. I'm sure farmers won't be budgeting on higher prices for the coming season," he said.
